content: A Pap smear is a microscopic examination of cells collected from the cervix, which is the lower part of the uterus that connects to the vagina. This test is primarily used to screen for cervical cancer. During the procedure, the patient lies on an examination table with their feet placed in stirrups. A healthcare provider inserts a speculum into the vagina to gently open it and visualize the cervix. Cells are then carefully scraped from the cervix and sent to a laboratory for analysis. Pap smears are essential for detecting cervical cancer early. Routine screening should begin at age 21. After the initial test: Women should undergo a Pap smear every two years to screen for cervical cancer. Women over 30 or those with three consecutive negative Pap smears may only need the test every three years. Women with new sexual partners, or whose partners have new sexual partners, should continue testing every two years. After the age of 65-70, most women can stop Pap smears if they have had three negative tests in the past 10 years. However, if a new sexual partner is introduced after this age, screening should resume. Women who have had a total hysterectomy (removal of the uterus and cervix) and have no history of cervical dysplasia, cervical cancer, or other pelvic cancers may not need further Pap smears. To prepare for a Pap smear, inform your healthcare provider if you are taking any medications, including birth control pills, have had an abnormal Pap smear in the past, or suspect you might be pregnant. Avoid douching, sexual intercourse, bathing, or using tampons for 24 hours before the test. It is also recommended to avoid scheduling the test during menstruation, as this can affect the accuracy of the results. If you are experiencing abnormal bleeding, your doctor may still advise proceeding with the test. Empty your bladder before the procedure. Light bleeding may occur afterward. The Pap smear is not 100% accurate, and in rare cases, cervical cancer may be missed. However, cervical cancer typically develops slowly, and follow-up Pap smears can detect concerning changes in time for treatment. Inform your doctor about all medications you are taking, as some, such as estrogen or progestins, may influence the test results. A normal Pap smear result indicates no abnormal cells are present. However, normal value ranges can vary slightly between laboratories, so it is important to discuss your specific results with your doctor. Abnormal Pap smear results are categorized as follows: ASCUS or AGUS (Atypical Cells of Uncertain Significance): These changes may be caused by an HPV infection or could indicate precancerous changes. LSIL (Low-Grade Dysplasia) or HSIL (High-Grade Dysplasia): These findings suggest precancerous changes, with a higher risk of cervical cancer associated with HSIL. Carcinoma in Situ (CIS): This indicates abnormal changes that are likely to progress to cancer. Atypical Squamous Cells (ASC-H): This suggests abnormal changes that may be consistent with HSIL. Atypical Glandular Cells (AGC): These changes may indicate precancerous conditions in the upper cervical canal or inside the uterus. If abnormal changes are detected, further testing or follow-up is required. The next steps depend on the Pap smear results, your previous history of Pap smears, and your risk factors for cervical cancer. Additional tests may include: A colposcopy-directed biopsy to examine the cervix more closely. An HPV test to identify high-risk HPV types associated with cervical cancer. For minor cell changes, a repeat Pap smear is often recommended in 3-6 months.
